title: A New Clue to the Puzzle of the Expanding Universe
summary:
Scientists know the universe is expanding, but they disagree about how fast. Two of the best ways to measure the speed disagree. This is the Hubble tension.

One way uses the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang. It predicts an expansion rate of about 67. The other way measures how fast faraway galaxies move away from us, using exploding stars called supernovae. Hubble and James Webb space telescope observations give a higher value of about 73. The gap is statistically very significant.

A team of researchers wondered whether tiny magnetic fields from the very early universe could help. They are called primordial magnetic fields. The idea is that they changed how the first hydrogen formed. That would shift the moment the universe became transparent and change the "cosmic ruler" used to measure distances.

The team ran three-dimensional simulations and tested them against observations. Their idea stayed possible. They found a mild preference for these fields, which they say is not yet a discovery, but a meaningful hint.
why_it_matters: The puzzle suggests that scientists' best model of the universe may be missing something, so solving it could change how we understand the universe.
